Text:
[TASK AND CREATION]
Use real campaign events as the skeleton of a medieval broadsheet story with vivid scenes and distinctive people. The main report must develop a concrete, complete, retellable incident around the lead event. Merely restating facts or adding decorative dialogue does not complete the task.

[INDEPENDENT INVENTION]
- Independently invent actions, brief dialogue, on-scene reactions, private arguments, embarrassment, misunderstandings, clever responses and everyday details absent from the material. They do not each need a factual source. Integrate them naturally without labeling every sentence as rumor or unverified.
- Make the incident plausible for the participants, period and world, with a setup, a development and a payoff. Reveal character through actions and speech rather than lists of personality traits.
- Preserve confirmed actors, places, times, actions and outcomes. Do not change victory, survival, wounds, captivity, relationship values, territory or executed diplomatic outcomes, or invent casualty figures. Invented anecdotes do not change game mechanics; never replace explicitly recorded dialogue or last words. Declarations and promises remain statements, not executed outcomes.
- Never reuse, allude to or rename the participants of real or potentially private player conversations to create fiction. Never claim an invented incident comes from player private conversations, letters or confidential records.

[ORGANIZATION AND LENGTH]
- Follow the system length of 330 to 500 words in three to five paragraphs for the main report. Make the first major event the main thread, with room for its incident to develop rather than dividing the space equally into short notices.
- Include every supplied major event in this same report. Connect related events naturally; incorporate unrelated major events through shifts of place, time or viewpoint without omitting them or inventing causal links.
- Open with an action, short remark, telling detail or aftermath, then naturally establish people, place, events and outcomes. Do not follow a fixed background-event-impact template; the setup, development and payoff need not be narrated in that order.
- End on a concrete consequence, a person's reaction or a meaningful detail. Do not force a political verdict unsupported by the situation.

[VOICE AND DELIVERY]
- Choose tension, absurdity, satire, indignity, courage, wit or dignity to suit the event. Do not require conflict, jokes or conspiracies. War, diplomacy, feasts, tournaments, policy and rebellion should have different viewpoints and rhythms.
- Keep dialogue brief and appropriate to medieval roles. Let actions and narration carry the story instead of continuous scripted conversation. Avoid modern internet jokes, empty claims that the world was shaken, ornate adjective piles and repeated battlefield cliches.
- Before delivering, check silently: is this merely a factual restatement? Does the incident develop and resolve? Do people act in concrete ways? Have confirmed outcomes been changed? Repair the draft within this response without showing the review.
- Use exactly [TITLE], [MAJOR], [M1]... and [SHORT]. Keep minor news brief; [SHORT] extracts only an anecdote already in the body. Add no extra sections, explanations or Markdown fences. Retain the battle-number, sally-out and territory-transfer rules.
